Macquarie says bank admitted failure
Macquarie Bank said it will not contest the ASIC proceeding and is expected to pay a $14 million civil penalty.
It said the ASIC announcement related to products offered on its website between December 2021 and September 2022.
It said the bank will admit to a contravention of its obligation to ensure it provides financial services efficiently, honestly and fairly.
"Macquarie's website offered a Welcome Rate on its Macquarie Savings Account," the bank's said in a statement.

"The matter arose because, when standard variable rates increased and exceeded the Welcome Rate, customers were instead paid the higher standard variable rate though some expected a bonus margin over that rate.
"Macquarie acknowledges that some of the wording on its website was not sufficiently clear and may have caused confusion."

Macquarie's head of banking and financial services Ben Perham said the bank's customers high expectations of it, "and although ASIC has acknowledged our actions were not deliberate, we should have better explained on our website how the Welcome Rate would be applied and we apologise for any confusion caused."

"We received some customer complaints regarding the description of the Welcome Rate on our website, and we elected to pay $8.8 million in compensation to put customers in the position that they would have been if the Welcome Rate was a fixed bonus interest margin," he said.
"Additionally, we have conducted a thorough review of all product descriptions we use across our website."
ASIC Commissioner Alan Kirkland said, "banks must get the basics right, which includes having systems and processes that deliver on the promises they make to customers".
"This wasn't just unclear wording," Mr Kirkland said.
"Macquarie's systems and controls were not rigorous enough to identify the risk that customers would misunderstand how the Welcome Rate worked.
"At a time when Australians are contending with cost-of-living pressures, consumers deserve clear information about savings rates and the financial benefits they are promised."
The proposed resolution is subject to the Court's approval.
McGrathNicol applying to extend David Jones admin process
David Jones administrator McGrathNicol has given the beleagured department store's creditors until next Monday to submit their proofs of debt.

The callout, which was sent out with a swaddle of documents late yesterday afternoon, is likely to see thousands of small to large businesses come forward with claims, from fashion brands to major landlords.
It's all ahead of the first creditors meeting next Tuesday, which will be held remotely.
There's also now just days left for other entities to put in expressions of interest to buy David Jones, with McGrathNicol already talking up interest in the 188-year old Australian retailer.
They have noted
We intend to lodge an application with the NSW Supreme Court to extend the convening period, providing additional time to undertake a sale and / or recapitalisation process for David Jones Group.

If the convening period is extended, the Administrators’ report to creditors and the second meeting of creditors will be held at a later date. We will write to creditors providing further details of any extension that is granted by the Supreme Court.
Yesterday, ABC News confirmed that David Jones was up to date with its superannuation payments to its 6,000 employees, in line with new "pay day" laws that started in July.
Key Event
Macquarie admits to breaking law over savings rates
Macquarie Bank has admitted to failures in the promotion of its "welcome" interest rate for new savings account customers.
The bank has admitted to breaching the Corporations Act and could face a $14 million penalty in proceedings brought by ASIC.
Macquarie described its welcome rate as a "welcome variable rate" and a "bonus", which ASIC alleges could lead customers to believe it was paid on top of the standard variable rate.
In fact, the welcome rate generally operated as a fixed rate that applied instead of, rather than in addition to, the standard rate during the four-month promotional period, the regulator said.

The penalty, which the parties have jointly proposed to the NSW Supreme Court, comes in addition to $8.8 million in remediation initiated by Macquarie, which has already been paid to nearly 40,000 customers.
Key Event
Wall Street closes in the red
The final numbers are in for Wall Street's session, with all key indices dragged down by inflation numbers that reinforced expectations the Federal Reserve will hike interest rates again soon.
The tech-centric Nasdaq shed 0.7%, after falling as much as 1.7% in early-afternoon trading, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average and the benchmark S&P 500 closed down 0.3% and 0.4%, respectively.
US 10-year Treasury yields jumped to 4.99%, while the US dollar jumped around 0.7% versus a basket of key currencies.
Key Event
CBA posts flat Q1 earnings
The CBA has posted a flat Q1 earnings update.
The bank's unaudited cash post tax profit came in at $2.8 billion, flat versus the quarterly average for the second half of FY2026, but up 8% on the corresponding quarter last year.
Operating income rose by 3% driven by lending and deposit growth, while operating expenses also rose by 3% due to wage and IT costs.
Loan impairment charges were also higher.
An impairment expense of $300 million (or 11bps of total loans) was booked. Collective provisions increased by $105 million over the quarter, but the bank says credit quality remains sound.
Home loan arrears also ticked higher by 7 bps ,which the bank says reflects cost-of-living pressures from higher inflation and interest rates.
Corporate troublesome and non-performing loan exposures were slightly higher at $6.9 billion, or around 1% of total loan exposures.

Anthropic eyes $US1.4 trillion IPO valuation

Anthropic's blockbuster IPO will value the Claude chatbot creator at up to $US1.4 trillion ($2.0 trillion), slightly short of some investors' expectations, setting up a key test of Wall Street's faith in the AI boom it helped ignite.

The company is kicking off the roadshow for a share sale expected to set a benchmark for the sector, following years of hype that fuelled a massive influx of capital into AI companies and sent the US stock market to all-time highs.

Anthropic's owners are ploughing ahead despite a recent sell-off across the tech landscape, as investors question whether the AI boom's returns will justify the massive spending and mounting debt costs in an elevated interest-rate environment.

The AI lab and some of its existing shareholders are aiming to raise up to $US64.4 billion ($93.8 billion) in the IPO by selling 825 million shares priced between $US70 and $US78 each. Shares are expected to start trading on the Nasdaq on November 19.

Anthropic will also raise $US26 billion ($37.9 billion) via a separate private placement deal with cornerstone investors, including Alphabet's Google, Nvidia— whose CEO is subject to a probe over his affair with an alleged Chinese spy — and Advanced Micro Devices.
The IPO is the year's most closely watched since Elon Musk's SpaceX, which raised $US75 billion ($109.2 billion) at a nearly $US1.75 trillion ($2.6 trillion) valuation in June.
Investors are raising concerns over the sustainability of the investment cycle, particularly around how quickly companies can turn their investments into revenue.

At the top of the price range, Anthropic would be valued at about $US1.4 trillion on a fully diluted basis, which includes securities such as stock options and restricted stock. On a non-diluted basis, excluding those securities, Anthropic's market value would be about $US1 trillion.

Key Event
Wall Street falls on hot inflation
Higher than expected inflation not only took the wind out of Wall Street's rally, it blew the markets backwards as betting firmed on a rate hike from the Fed next month.
Interest rate markets have now fully priced in a hike at the Fed's December meeting after the US CPI came it at 0.4% growth in October, compared with expectations of 0.3%.
It's the third consecutive month of inflation coming in at 0.4% or above. It was 0.6% in September.
At 7:30am AEDT
• Nasdaq: -0.7%
The negative sentiment was reinforced by two senior (voting) Fed members openly talking about the need to raise rates, putting the idea of a 50bp hike in traders' minds.
That sent US bond yields and the US dollar higher, while the Aussie dollar fell almost 1% to 68.63 US cents.
Futures trading points to the ASX 200 falling around 0.5% today after yesterday's solid 1.1% rally.
On Wall Street, tech stocks were again under pressure.

The S&P 500 technology sector dropped around 1% as the worst performing of the 11 major sectors, weighed down by another drop in Nvidia, which fell more than 5% and has tumbled about 10% over the past two sessions.
The company's stock reflects mounting concerns over CEO Jensen Huang's future at the chip company after it initiated an internal probe into spy claims involving Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang.
Investors are also bracing for Anthropic's expected public listing later this month.
The AI lab revealed that its initial public offering is expected to raise as much as $US64.4 billion, giving the company a fully diluted valuation of up to $US1.4 trillion.
A listing by Anthropic could also force other AI heavyweights to compete harder for investor dollars.
On commodity markets, gold fell almost 3% on the inflation data release while oil prices eased further to a two-month low.
